utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, ladies and gentlemen; good morning to the technical booth, the interpreters; good morning to the legal assistants and the court reporters, the registrar, the Prosecution; good morning, Mr. Harmon, Mr. Cayley, Mr. McCloskey; good morning to the Defence counsel: Mr. Visnjic, Mr. Petrusic; good morning, General Krstic. We are here today to resume our case, and I believe there was a question related to the tendering of documents. So I turn to Mr. McCloskey. Do we have some exhibits to deal with relating to Mr. Richard Butler's testimony?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, counsel. Yes, we do. Prior to getting into that, could we go into private session briefly so I can explain just a situation that occurred at the last day of Mr. Butler's testimony that we had some concern about?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, let us go into private session for a few minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are in public session, so we can continue with our proceedings. Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I have an exhibit, one more exhibit, 394, which is a list of all the exhibits that Mr. Butler referred to, and I would just provide it as sort of a last exhibit to the Court so we don't have to go and list every exhibit, and in combination with it is a two-page -- or excuse me, a three-page document which lists all the exhibits that should be under seal. And both the Exhibit 394 and the under seal list has been provided to the registry, and it is all those exhibits that we wish to tender into evidence. The Defence has been provided with that list, and we've had a chance to speak with them briefly. And could this Exhibit 394 be under seal as well since it has some sensitive information on it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Petrusic, do you have any objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, in view of the fact that Exhibit 394 is a list of exhibits tendered by -- produced by Mr. Butler, it is rather long, so the Defence will not go into each individual exhibit on that list, but it will analyse them by accepting some exhibits without any objection and making objections regarding another set of exhibits, so that according to a methodology that we would like to propose, it would be more appropriate to refer first to the exhibits to which the Defence objects. Therefore, if this exhibit is marked as 394 by the registrar, and I see that it is, then allow me to say which are the exhibits that the Defence objects to. They are numbers 438 through to 452; then from 470 to 480; also from numbers 500 through to 531; from number 551 through to 565; also from number 598 to 608; from Exhibit 620 to 625, as well as numbers 630 to 638. We also object to Exhibits 650 through to 674, as well as exhibits from 677 through to 692 -- no, sorry, I beg your pardon. I'm so sorry, from 677 to 692, and from number 695 to 701. Our objections to these exhibits are based on the same arguments as our objection regarding the transcript of the 27th of June during the proceedings. If the Chamber so desires, our objection was based on the method in which the conversations were intercepted. If necessary, the Defence can elaborate on that objection which would basically be the same objection as has been recorded in the transcript on the 27th of June. Regarding the other exhibits included in this list 394, the Defence has no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. These intercepts were listed on this list merely so as a record of which intercepts Mr. Butler particularly referred to. It is my understanding that the Court has already ruled on all these intercepts and that they've already been admitted into evidence. I think counsel has implied that in his question, also. We're not aware of any new intercepts. As far as we know, we have not offered any new intercepts, and I can be firm on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Petrusic, we have a question for you. In relation to the previous decision, do you have any elements of a different nature or anything else to say, or is your objection the same objection that you made to this Chamber previously, prior to our previous decision?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, in view of the fact that these are the same kinds of documents or, rather, the same exhibits on which the Chamber has ruled, the Defence has nothing else to point out except for the reasons already given.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We would like to review all those documents again, but if there is nothing new, then we will repeat the decision. However, we would like to reserve a little bit of time, perhaps until the end of this morning, to review the documents and to see if there is any difference or not. So we'll reserve our decision until the end of the morning. Maybe it's not necessary now to separate the documents to which an objection has been made and those in regard to which there are no objections. So we will reserve our decision until the end of the morning regarding the whole list of documents. However, in the meantime we can now proceed with the testimony planned for today.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. One last issue Ms. Keith reminds me of. I referred to an exhibit as 638/1A, and as counsel pointed out to us last week, that should be 638/A. With that, I will give the floor to Mr. Cayley.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours, Mr. Petrusic, Mr. Visnjic. If I could just be given a moment, Your Honour, to arrange my papers and then we can proceed. Yes. Thank you, Mr. President. If it pleases the Court, with your permission, if we could call the next witness, Major General Richard Dannatt.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, General Dannatt. Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I can. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Will you please read the solemn declaration that the usher will give you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You may be seated now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: First of all, let me thank you for having come here to testify before the International Criminal Tribunal. You will first be answering questions that Mr. Cayley is going to put to you. Mr. Cayley is on your right-hand side. Mr. Cayley, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Examined by Mr. Cayley:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, your name is Francis Richard Dannatt; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT
utterances.text: Yes, sir, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your last name is spelled D-a-n-n-a-t-t.

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, could you move the ELMO, because at the moment the witness and I are looking through a solid objective at each other. Thank you. That's perfect. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You are British.

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT
utterances.text: I am British.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were born in 1950.

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You are presently a Major General in the British Army, commanding the 3rd United Kingdom Division based in Bulford in the United Kingdom.

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT
utterances.text: That's correct. The headquarters of the division is based in Bulford.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just to remind you, General, as we spoke previously, you and I speak the same language and between us there are interpreters. I will try to speak as slowly as I can, also to keep a reasonable pace. If you could pause between my question and your answer, and I will do the same for you, that will facilitate the work of the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT
utterances.text: That's understood.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, you were consulted by the Office of the Prosecutor as an expert in this case and we asked you about three specific areas on which you produced a written report, which has been given to the Defence and, indeed, to the Judges. Could you summarise for the Judges essentially the three principal areas that we asked you to give your opinion upon?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I can. I was first asked to speak about military doctrine; the doctrines and methods of military command and control generally, and with specific reference to the army of Republika Srpska, the VRS, and even more specifically with reference to the Drina Corps. I was also asked to comment on command and control responsibilities; the roles and responsibilities of a Corps Commander and the Corps Chief of Staff generally, and again with specific reference to the VRS and the Drina Corps. Also, thirdly, command and control as far as operations are concerned; issues relating to operational and logistic planning, tactical tempo, and the headquarters' command and control procedures relevant to this case.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In a sense, you are giving a strategic or bird's-eye view of matters relevant to this case; would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT
utterances.text: It's my endeavour to do that, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, what qualifies you to give these opinions to this Court?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT
utterances.text: First, I have 31 years' experience in the British Army. I have served on operations in every rank from 2nd Lieutenant to Major General, and I shall perhaps return to that later, what those different responsibilities have been. I've also spent time as a student at the British Army Staff College and also on the staff of the British Army Staff College where I ran the Higher Command and Staff course which is particularly responsible for teaching the operational level of war, that is, the campaign level of war. Also, while I was fulfilling that appointment, I was required to produce a new War Fighting Doctrine for the British Army in the immediate years following the end of the Cold War, which required me to do considerable research into military command and control before writing that War Fighting Doctrine. In the end, two documents were produced: a War Fighting Doctrine as Volume I, which I was the lead author for, and then secondly, another document which specialised in command and control and I was on the consultative panel to assist the specific author of that document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, in assisting in this volume concerning command and control, did you study command and control doctrines of armies around the world?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT
utterances.text: Yes, I did. As part of the studies of the Higher Command and Staff course initially, which I attended that course as a student before I became the director of it, part and parcel of the syllabus is the study of other armies' command and control procedures. This, for me, was a very useful background before I began writing the War Fighting Doctrine to which I've just referred.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, let's speak a little about your career in some detail to confirm what you've already said about commanding at all levels in the British Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If Prosecutor's Exhibit 395 could be placed on the ELMO next to General Dannatt, that will assist him in this part of his testimony.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, General, while that's being placed on the ELMO, I think traditionally, as with all British officers, you attended the Royal Military Academy Sandhurst from 1969 to 1971 as a young cadet officer; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT
utterances.text: That's correct. I joined the army straight from school in 1969 and spent two years at the Royal Military Academy Sandhurst to equal myself to become a regular officer and commissioned into my regiment in July 1971.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry to interrupt you, but I think that the ELMO and other equipment seems not to enjoy weekends. Is it possible to do something to improve the quality of the image?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, as much as I realise this is not -- does not facilitate the public gallery in viewing it, might I suggest that if we place copies in front of Your Honours and proceed -- Defence counsel also have copies -- rather than taking a break so we can move ahead with General Dannatt's testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Mr. Cayley. We agree with you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, Prosecutor's Exhibit 395 has been placed on the ELMO. Unfortunately, the image is not very satisfactory that's coming up on the television screens, but if you can give a brief synopsis using this exhibit of your career from 1971 to date, please.

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT
utterances.text: Yes, I'm very happy to do that. As I mentioned just now, I commissioned in 1971 and joined my regiment, an infantry regiment known as the Green Howards, and assumed command of a platoon. There are three platoons in a company, and I commanded one of those platoons. I joined my regiment at the start of an operational tour in Northern Ireland in August 1971. I remained in command of that platoon for some two years doing two tours of operational duty in Belfast, Northern Ireland, as well as exercises in our main NATO role in Germany, including a large exercise in Canada. In 1973, I then went to university and spent three years at the University of Durham where I read a degree in economic history. On return from university, I went back to my battalion as the adjutant, which is the principle Staff Officer to the Commanding Officer, if you like, the kind of Chief of Staff to the Commanding Officer within a regiment of the British Army. Having fulfilled that post, from 1976 to 1979 I returned to the Royal Military Academy Sandhurst as an instructor and spent two years instructing officer cadets in general military tactics and what they needed to know to be professional army officers. Briefly in 1981, I returned to my regiment and assumed command of a company. There are three rifle companies in an infantry regiment, and I assumed command of one of those companies, and during that time, as well as normal training, carried out an operational tour with the United Nations in Cyprus. At the end of 1981 I returned to the Staff College where I was a student at the British Army Staff College through 1982. On leaving the Staff College in 1982, I became the Chief of Staff of one of the British armoured brigades based in Germany. And a brigade shown on the diagram here, is a grouping of three or four combat units of battalion size such as I had served in before, and also a grouping that includes artillery, engineers, signals, logistics, a grouping of 4.000 to 5.000 troops. And as a Major of, I was the Chief of Staff from 1983 to 1984. In 1985 I returned back to my battalion and once again commanded a company of The Green Howards, my own regiment. At the end of 1986 I was posted to the Ministry of Defence in London where I was the military assistant to one of our Defence ministers, the Minister of State for the Armed Forces in London for three years, from 1986 to 1989. After that, I was appointed to command my own regiment, therefore became Battalion Commander in the rank of Lieutenant Colonel in 1989, an appointment I held through to the end of 1991. That included another operational tour in Northern Ireland. At the beginning of 1992, I returned to the Staff College as a student on the Higher Commander Staff course which was the course that I mentioned earlier, and at the end of that four-month course I then became the director of that course and stayed for another two years running the two successive courses that then followed, and it was during that period that I wrote the War Fighting Doctrine, again, that I referred to earlier. At the beginning of 1984, I was then posted back to Germany and assumed command of the 4th Armoured Brigade, one of the three British armoured brigades in Germany.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, can I interrupt you? You said, you said at the beginning of 1984, and I think you meant at the beginning of 1994.

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT
utterances.text: You're quite correct, yes. 1994 I assumed command of 4th Armoured Brigade and retained command of that brigade through until early 1996. And during that period, I took the brigade to the former Republic of Yugoslavia where I was the United Nations Sector Commander in sector southwest with my headquarters in Gornji Vakuf from October 1995 until the implementation of the Dayton Peace Agreement in December of that year, at which point I resumed my NATO, my British appointment, of Commander 4th Armoured Brigade and began the process of implementing the terms of the Dayton Peace Agreement on the ground in southwest Bosnia, and continued doing that until the end of April 1996. In the middle of 1996, I handed over command of 4th Armoured Brigade and returned to the Ministry of Defence where I filled the appointment of defence -- of director of the Defence Programme staff, which meant that I had some responsibility with my civil service colleagues for allocating the funds between the army, navy, and the air force. I remained in that post until the beginning of last year, January of 1999, when I assumed command of the 3rd United Kingdom Division, the post that I currently hold. And the 3rd United Kingdom Division is a division based with its headquarters in Bulford in the United Kingdom. There are four constituent brigades in that division, all based in the United Kingdom, three mechanised brigades and one reconnaissance brigade, with a total strength of around 20.000 peacetime establishment which would expand to some 30.000 on mobilisation for war. And that is the present -- the appointment that I currently hold.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, just to give an idea of numbers to the Judges, when you commanded a platoon, how many men were under your command?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT
utterances.text: A platoon is approximately 35 men; and a company, I judge to be your next question, sir, is about 100 to 120 men; and a battalion is between 600 and 800 men, depending on the role that a battalion is fulfilling at the time; and a brigade is between 4.000 and 5.000 men, and I've just mentioned that my current division is about 20.000 men.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, next year I believe you have been selected and, indeed, appointed to the position of the Assistant Chief of the General Staff of the British Army; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT
utterances.text: That's correct. I shall move to that position sometime yet to be specified in the middle of next year.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, finally, on your biographical details, I see that you're wearing the military cross. You were decorated for gallantry on operations in Northern Ireland in 1973; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT
utterances.text: That's correct, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I think you were made a Commander of the Order of the British Empire in 1996 for your services in the former Yugoslavia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT
utterances.text: That's also correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I think that you have also received the Queen's commendation for valuable service in Kosovo; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT
utterances.text: That's correct. When I was going through my former service, I didn't mention that last year I was Commander British forces in Kosovo in the central section of the initial operations there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in fact, on that point, in June and July of last year, you deployed your divisional headquarters to Kosovo and, in fact, were Commander British forces NATO KFOR last year; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT
utterances.text: I was Commander British forces, and my task was to maximise the British support to NATO's KFOR, yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, General, really finally in terms of biographical details, you are a British Army officer. General Krstic is a JNA and VRS officer. There are many similarities between your careers. You're both professional officers, but you grew up in very different systems. If Prosecutor's Exhibit 396 could be placed upon the ELMO, and I'll give you the question while the exhibit is coming. On the basis of what I've just said, General, what gives you the right to comment on those matters that you've already stated to the Judges that the Prosecutor asked you to address?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, do you have this in front of you because it's actually quite an important document? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT
utterances.text: I think first within all professional and well-trained armies there are a number of general principles of command and control that apply that from my studies of a number of armies, I recognise both within my own army and also within the army of the former Yugoslavia. But probably rather more specifically, and having looked at General Krstic's former career up to this stage, I notice a number of similarities between himself and myself which I've shown on this exhibit. We're roughly the same age; General Krstic is two years older than myself. He has been a Battalion Commander. He has been a Brigade Chief of Staff, both posts that I have held. He has been a Brigade Commander. He was promoted to Major General some three or four years ahead of myself being promoted Major General. And I now command a division, and he commanded a corps, and my understanding of the Drina Corps was that in manpower terms, it broadly equated to the size of command that I currently hold as a Divisional Commander. I'm also aware that there's a slight difference in rank and the naming of ranks between the VRS and the British army, and that I am a Major General, which we would call a two-star general. A Lieutenant General in the British Army is a three star. I believe in the VRS the equivalent ranks are effectively one star lower. So I believe that there are a number of broad comparisons, both in terms of appointments that I have held and General Krstic has held that qualify me to offer some opinions that would be of some use to the Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If the witness could be given Exhibit 397 which actually helps to explain this slight difference in the ranking structure so that the Judges can understand perfectly what you're speaking about in these terms. Again, unfortunately the ELMO is not working, but nevertheless, General, if you could briefly explain Exhibit 397.

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT
utterances.text: Within the British Army, a battalion is commanded by a Lieutenant Colonel, and my understanding in the VRS is that usually a battalion was commanded by a Major. Again, in the British Army a brigade is commanded by a Brigadier or, as somebody would call it, a one-star General, but in the VRS, brigades are invariably commanded by a Colonel. In the British Army, a two-star General, who is a Major General, commands a division; the equivalent formation within the VRS is a corps commanded by a Major General. This would seem to equate to a one-star General, the equivalent in rank in British terms of a Brigadier. In the British Army, above division is a corps commanded by a Lieutenant General, a three-star General. There is no direct equivalent, as far as I can discover, in the VRS. At the highest level, there is an army, or an army group in the British Army, which is a number of corps commanded by a full General, a four-star General, and that equivalent grouping in the VRS army is commanded by a Colonel General. Interestingly, the French army, for example, very aptly describe by function General du Brigade, General du Division; but rather the same as the VRS, officers were one rank above that which they equate to in NATO. A number of armies have a slightly different equivalence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, General, you said that there was no equivalent to a Lieutenant General although, in fact, in the VRS, I think you may mention it in your report, there is a Lieutenant Colonel-General which is a two-star rank, essentially; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, if during General Dannatt's testimony you wish to ask any questions for clarification, please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Can I just ask whether or not in the VRS, the top rank, army, Colonel General, is that what Mladic was?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT
utterances.text: My understanding is that that is correct, yes, a senior appointment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, what materials have been supplied to you by the Office of the Prosecutor in order for you to come to your conclusions and, indeed, prepare your report and your testimony?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT
utterances.text: A number of documents have been made available to me. I have seen the two reports by Richard Butler; one entitled "The VRS Corps Command Responsibility Study" and the second, "The Srebrenica Military Narrative Krivaca 95." I've seen and asked to see and been shown much of the documentary evidence in support of those reports. I'm aware that those reports are derivative pieces of work and I've asked to see selected documents which underpin both those reports. I've also seen a number of maps and other documents and video footage pertaining to these issues generally. I also asked, as my previous service in Bosnia had not taken me to the area of Srebrenica, to go and visit the various locations and places germane to the matters before the Court. In April this year, I visited those principal locations with senior investigator, Mr. Jean-Rene Ruez, and also with Mr. Cayley from the Office of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think as well, General, you've viewed certain maps in the possession of the Prosecutor, some video footage, and indeed, as you rightly said, documents that you've requested to see from us; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT
utterances.text: That's absolutely correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: These are all items, Your Honours, that indeed the Defence have had sight of or have seen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, if we can turn to the first substantive part of your report which deals with fundamental principles of command and control, and you'll find that on page 4 of your report. Could you explain to the Judges the basic principle of command and control that, from your understanding, is of universal application to all armies of the world?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I will. I think first, the first overall principle, and it's an obvious one, is that Superior Commanders give orders to their subordinate Commanders who carry out those orders and implement them. Now, of course, the manner of implementation may allow a greater or a lesser degree of interpretation or useful initiative according to the command doctrine, the method of command used by a particular army. In the case of the VRS, the superior-subordinate relationship is laid down quite clearly in a number of documents, and that particular principle is well-established. The second basic principle is that subordinates must report upwards the results of their actions to inform their superiors of progress or otherwise in order for the higher command to know what's going on, to be informed, and for itself to take subsequent decisions to order subsequent activities. In some armies, reporting is by exception. In other words, if things are going well, you don't need to keep an endless pattern of reports going. But it's a basic duty of all subordinates to keep the passage of information moving upwards so that decision-making can be facilitated by the higher headquarters. I think those are the two underlying principles that govern all military operations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, General, in your written report, you identify two principal command doctrines which are practiced in armies of the world, and the first one that you give a brief synopsis upon, and forgive me for murdering the German, is the military doctrine of Auftragstaktik. Can you explain to the Judges the meaning of this and give an example of an army which adopts this command doctrine?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT
utterances.text: Yes, I can. We use two terms to describe the two principal schools of command philosophy. One of those terms is the one you just used, Auftragstaktik, I'll explain that, and the other term is another German word called Befehlstaktik, and I'll explain that. Under the doctrine --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Excuse me. Could you repeat this, please.

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT
utterances.text: The two words are -- they're both German words, Auftragstaktik, and the other word is Befehlstaktik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT
utterances.text: The Germans are always very precise in their definition of these things, and that is why we tend to use those two words in the sort of parlance of military command and control to describe those two schools of thought. Under the doctrine known as Auftragstaktik, this is a doctrine whereby a Superior Commander decides what his mission is and sets out his broad intent to his subordinates and then gives them considerable latitude in the way in which they carry out that mission. Obviously, the Superior Commander provides certain resources, what he believes are adequate resources, to the subordinate - manpower, equipment, logistic support, and so forth - but gives him considerable freedom to use his initiative to carry out his task. For example, in very general terms, the mission might be, couched in generic terms such as, "Capture hill A in order to cross river B." Now, what that says to the subordinate Commander is that, yes, he's got to capture hill A but then the purpose beyond that is so that the army can then advance across the river. So it may be that when he looks at the situation, hill A perhaps is no longer very relevant. What matters most is actually getting across the river. So he'll use his initiative to find a better way to actually carry out that mission. In the British Army, this is the doctrine that we espouse; a number of NATO armies espouse that doctrine. In English words, it's a doctrine called Mission Command but it's derived from this term, Auftragstaktik. By contrast, the other doctrine under the German label -- the German word, Befehlstaktik, is a much more specific system of command and control whereby orders are given by the Superior Commander to the subordinate. They are detailed and subordinates are expected to fulfil them as specified. So the order to capture hill A would be carried out, and then a subsequent order would be expected to be given, "Advance towards river B and cross at bridge C," and that would be specifically done. Armies which adopt one or other method of command and control tend to be characterised as to whether they are professional armies or whether they are conscripted armies. A conscripted army, which only has soldiers for a short period of time and can only develop their training to a limited extent, tend to follow this more restrictive form of command known as Befehlstaktik. For example, in the British Army, in the early part of the Second World War when the British Army had to very rapidly expand from being the small standing army that it was in the '30s to a large army through a mass process of conscription, it was an army that was characterised by Befehlstaktik-type of command and control. General Montgomery, for example, when he conducted the attack at El Alamein in 1942 laid down very specifically what the corps and the divisions were actually to do and when they were to do it in order to achieve the objectives. He did not leave very much to chance or to initiative lower down. He liked, what he called, "a tidy battlefield." Interestingly and by contrast, the German Army, although it had had to expand also rapidly in the '30s, followed the Auftragstaktik method of command. Particularly in the western dessert in 1942 and 1943, subordinate Commanders used their initiative in very imaginative ways and often outmaneuvered the rather more static and procedural British forces. I think those that have studied military history at all will know that the classic example of this Auftragstaktik, outmaneuvering tactic, was used to great effect by the Germans in 1940 in the so-called Blitzkrieg campaign, when German armoured forces crossed the Meuse, broke through the British and French lines, got deep into their rear areas and achieved a stunning success well disproportionate to their actual strength. The secret of success there is that subordinates are allowed to use their initiative and not be over-controlled. Perhaps the issue and the application here, I think, is that the Befehlstaktik central control method is one that has been traditionally favoured by centralist states; was one favoured by the Warsaw Pact nations; was the one favoured by the army of the former Soviet Union and taught at its Staff Colleges and Staff Schools; large armies, conscripted armies. One sees the genesis of the command and control procedures followed by the old JNA, the old Yugoslav National Army, and the army of Republika Srpska in that basic tenet of centralised control of Befehlstaktik. I make that distinction that it's that centralist type of command and control that I see evidence of in the VRS with its antecedents, very strongly in the JNA, the former JNA.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, General, in your report at page 6, you say that as part of this doctrine of Befehlstaktik, that authority is not delegated; limitations are invariably imposed; the culture is one of seeking authority rather than taking decisions based on one's own authority. Does that mean in simple terms, General, that nothing really happens without orders coming from above in an army based on this kind of doctrine?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT
utterances.text: In general terms, that is correct. When you've got a centralised system, then almost by definition the man at the top or the men higher up are going to be the principle decision-makers and decision-takers and orders will be passed down. Of course, it goes back to something I was saying before, that that sort of system can only be properly implemented and made effective if there is an adequate flow of information coming up from the lower levels so that the higher level principal decision-takers know what is going on and can take those decisions. Of course, it would be wrong to suggest that no initiative can be used. We're not talking about an army of pure autonomy here. Initiative could be used in minor matters. But generally the system I'm referring to is characterised by significant decisions, the majority of decisions being taken at the higher level and those decisions then being passed down for implementation rather than for interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Could I ask one question along those lines, General Dannatt. Would it also be a characteristic of this kind of command and control, Befehlstaktik, for those orders from above to be usually written? I mean, is there any tradition or expected practice differentiating between written and oral orders depending upon the command and control or the flexibility of the subordinates?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT
utterances.text: An order is an order, whether it's written or spoken. Armies tend to be a little bureaucratic, so a lot does get written down. There's a bit of a feeling sometimes that if it's not written down, it's not really true or doesn't really have to happen, so often difficult orders are written down so that their understanding is clear and that the intent is properly communicated. But of course, without dwelling on this too long, under the Befehlstaktik-type of arrangement, you're going to find an operation order going into considerable detail about who should do what, who should go where; whereas under the maneuverist Auftragstaktik process, you can often launch quite a complicated or quite a large-scale operation perhaps with just a map and a number of lines on a map and a few notes down the side, because you're relying on the professional expertise of subordinates to understand the Higher Commander's intent, to interpret what he wants them to do, and get on with it. It doesn't need to be written down to quite the same extent. So the Befehlstaktik, central control, tends to show more actually written down.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Following on from Judge Wald's question, General, within the Befehlstaktik doctrine, there would be, and I ask this as a question, oral orders, presumably following on from a main operations order from a Commander, oral orders could be given to subordinates?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT
utterances.text: Yes. A normal process of the deliberate planning phase at the start of a major operation is for a Superior Commander to call together his principal subordinates and to go through an oral, spoken process of giving orders invariably following a set procedure and sequence of subjects. And that is then followed up by the issue of the written operation order which underpins and underlines everything that was said in the oral orders which -- the oral orders process is terribly important in order for a Superior Commander to communicate directly on a personal basis to his subordinates and to put some of his own character, some of his own determination and drive over during that process so they understand quite clearly what it is that he wants them to do. And also it's quite normal, as you would expect, at the end of an oral orders session for the Superior Commander to invite his subordinates to ask questions to clarify any points of detail that they might not have understood. And again, and I don't want to belabour this too much, the difference between the two systems would be that on the Befehlstaktik, the central command process, the subordinates would simply be seeking clarification that they've got it absolutely clear in their mind what tasks they've got to carry out. Under the Auftragstaktik, such as my army follows, what you're more likely to get at that stage of the oral orders are the subordinate Commanders telling the Superior Commander how they're going to carry out their mission, what it is that they're going to do. So they're telling him how they're going to do it as opposed to them -- the Higher Commander telling them what is to be done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Cayley, just one question. General, to have one system or another, to choose between the two, does that have anything to do with the level of training of officers? In other words, if I have very well-trained officers, I can choose between one of the two systems; if I have officers or soldiers who are not very well trained, would it be preferable for me to choose another one?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT
utterances.text: I think there are two parts to an answer that I could give to that, sir. First of all, an army is an institution, and it will have decided institutionally which of those two doctrines it is going to espouse at any one time, and that doctrine will be taught at the officer training schools, it will be taught at the Staff College, and that doctrine will persuade the army throughout, and that will be its chosen method of command and control. My second answer is that formal training in an understanding of doctrinal issues such as I am describing is predominately the business of Staff Colleges and going to affect more senior officers so that they have a clear understanding of the doctrinal route. A 2nd Lieutenant who is commanding a platoon gets on with his job in the general way that an army -- his army does its business. He won't necessarily understand that he is following a particular doctrine of one type or another, but that is the whole attitude of his army, and his training will have been governed by that attitude, although it will be taught formally higher up. And I think also related to that is something that I referred to earlier on, that when an army is a conscripted army and the soldiers are only there for a short period of time it is more naturally going to choose that much more directed and centralised method as opposed to an professional army. And if I was to, and I won't, go through the history of the British army, it has changed from time to time between one method and another, and we have followed the centralised during the periods of the First and Second World War when it was a conscripted army, but otherwise generally have followed the other doctrine when it's a small professional army where people knew each other and were well trained.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Excuse me. Just to be able to follow you up very closely, concerning the oral orders in the Befehlstaktik, you mentioned the Befehlstaktik gives the subordinates minute details, you mentioned even a map, but you said the oral orders -- you mentioned the oral orders process is terribly important. How can oral orders specify minute details if they have to follow it? As you mentioned, about General Montgomery's desert operation, can oral orders suffice then?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT
utterances.text: Oral orders could suffice, but those oral orders would probably be very lengthy and go on for really some time and would run the risk of error creeping in. So the complete solution to the planning process would be the production and issuing of a detailed written operation order which would specify all the subordinates their various tasks and their timings, and the coordination of one brigade with another and the artillery and the air force support and so on. But it's still important that there is a spoken, an oral order session, particularly so that the Commander himself can get over some of his character, can put over to his subordinates sort of the way that he wants to do it. The military business is a human business, and humans need to interact so that a subordinate understands the strength of intent of his subordinate and understands something of his character. So it's a two-way process.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you very much, General.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, you just stated at the end of your answer to Judge Riad that a subordinate needs to understand the strength of his intent of his subordinate, and I think you meant superior, did you not?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sorry, just to correct your --

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT
utterances.text: A junior officer has to understand what his senior wants, and do it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, you stated earlier that the Bosnian Serb army was based on the doctrine of the JNA Befehlstaktik. Why do you say this?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT
utterances.text: I said it for two reasons, really. One is having studied in a theoretical sense the origins of the army Republika Srpska, one can see its origins in a general and, in many ways, pretty specific sense in the army of the former Yugoslavia, the JNA. And although the former Yugoslavia was not a Warsaw Pact country, it was very much influenced by Eastern Block thinking, and one sees a lot of exchange of officers between the former Yugoslavia and the former Soviet Union, and the thinking of the former Soviet Union, the Befehlstaktik, the centralist thinking, in viewing itself in the army of the former JNA and in the army of Republika Srpska. So in a theoretical sense, I'm convinced that in general terms that that's where the VRS has its origins. In all practical sense, operating myself in Bosnia -- and of course I should also say that a number of former JNA officers didn't just form the framework of the VRS. To a certain extent and a lesser extent they formed the framework of the HVO, the Bosnian Croat army, and also the army of the Muslim government. Therefore, that's all centralist control one saw in all three of those armies. And operating on the ground, one saw several examples of the typical inflexibility that you get at low level when there is a centralist control in place, and that people at lower level are not prepared to use their initiative and will not let you do something that on the face of it would seem pretty sensible; but they are very much aware that they cannot give authority to do something without referring upwards to seek a higher authority, and it can be as small a thing as whether a particular vehicle can pass through a checkpoint because that soldier, that non-commissioned officer, has been told that no one is to pass through. There may be a very good reason why he perhaps should be allowed to pass through just a few hundred yards for some reason or other, but will not do so without referring up for a higher authority. And perhaps a more specific example I might give, if it's of interest to the Court, just before we began to implement the Dayton Peace agreement, and I've already mentioned I was already in Bosnia at that time, I knew that forces under my command, British forces, were going to be operating in Republika Srpska in the area controlled by the Serbs for the first time. And knowing that the Serbs had been defending in Western Bosnia for the previous few months very vigorously against the advance of Muslim and Croat forces, there was every likelihood, I felt, that when NATO force, British forces, my forces, started to move into Republika Srpska, this would not only be resented but could well be opposed by Serb soldiers; and therefore, I felt it was important to make sure that General Talic, who was the Commander of the 1st Krajina Corps, commanding in that area knew exactly what my plan was so that he could pass down his chain of command information about my plan and brief right down to the soldiers on the ground exactly at what time and in what place the NATO troops would be arriving. Now, I had to go to Banja Luka to try and find General Talic to brief him about this, which was not actually that easy to do. General Talic knew I was coming, but he wouldn't actually see me in person because he hadn't got authority from General Mladic to talk to this NATO officer. So I had to give my message through a colonel-level liaison officer. So although it was the sensible and logical thing to do for General Talic to see me, he wasn't prepared to see me because General Mladic hadn't given him authority to do so. However, my message I know was conveyed to General Talic because at the start of operations on the 21st of December when my troops crossed over the confrontation line into Republika Srpska, the soldiers on the ground knew we were coming. Information had been passed down their chain of command. They put their cleaner uniforms on. A tank that had been blocking the route that I wanted to advance on had been moved, as I'd asked it to be moved, so I knew that the command and control system was working and that they had effectively passed down from the General at the top right to the soldier on the ground the message that I wanted to pass. So that centralist system was very much alive and well at that stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, we've got used to sort of signalling each other about breaks. I thought you were signalling to me that now would be an appropriate time to have a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Cayley, I think it is the appropriate time before you go into your next question, so we'll have a half-hour break. Thank you very much for drawing my attention to the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Cayley, I think that the ELMO is here again.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. At the break I think the old one was declared dead so they've brought in a Barns Wallace creation which does work. But it would facilitate the public essentially seeing documents which I know is very important.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very good. There will be a death certificate issued for the ELMO, I suppose. I think that we can now proceed. Mr. Cayley, please continue.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, as you will see next to you, there is a video camera. The ELMO machine is not functioning. In order to facilitate the public seeing documents that we're going to use in your examination-in-chief, they will be put on the table. We may have to manoeuvre the table around, but it will at least enable public transmission of documents that you're going to refer to. Before we move on to the next area of your testimony, I want to come back briefly to a particular topic that you addressed in response to a question, I think, from Judge Wald. It was concerning the JNA, the constitution of the JNA, and you said that the JNA was a conscript army. The equivalent of commissioned officers, those of the rank from 2nd Lieutenant and above, were they conscripted or were they professionally trained officers?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT
utterances.text: I think what we saw and see is a corps of professional officers, a number of whom were mostly professional officers, were former JNA officers. The more senior ones had been through a formal staff process. And to that, obviously were added a number of officers and soldiers who, through the expediency of the situation and the fact they found themselves in a war situation, found themselves in the army. So on the one hand, you had a corps of professionally trained officers, but the majority of the army were locally recruited, effectively conscripted individuals.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say "a corps of professional officers, a number of whom were former JNA officers," here you're referring to those officers who subsequently went into the Bosnian Serb army; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT
utterances.text: That's correct. As I mentioned also earlier, one found in the army of the Bosnian Croats and the Bosnian Muslims a number of former JNA officers who, by inclination, had chosen to serve with those armies rather than another.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I'm right in saying that you have been spending time serving with the British Army, with UN and NATO forces, in the former Yugoslavia from 1994 to date except for the year 1998; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT
utterances.text: Yes, I've served at some stage or other in Bosnia-Herzegovina every year except 1998, since 1994. I first went to Sarajevo in February 1994 whether General Rose was the UN Commander there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think all in all you've spent just under a year in the former Yugoslavia during the last six years.

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT
utterances.text: The time aggregates to about that. The majority of it was in 1995 and 1996, and then a period of time last year; that aggregates to about a year.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Can I just ask a specification. When you said, "the majority of the army were effectively conscripted individuals," what is the meaning of "effectively conscripted individuals"?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT
utterances.text: By which I meant that the VRS was, in the main, a conscripted army; that people were called up from civilian life to become soldiers for the duration of the emergency. That was where the majority of their people came from, and that was based around a corps of professional officers --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: No previous training?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: No military education?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT
utterances.text: Well, obviously everybody is first and foremost a civilian and has to go through some process of training before they become a soldier. I think most of the people that were involved as soldiers in the VRS were civilians before the war, the civil war in the former Yugoslavia, began and had some training, probably rather less training than they would have liked to have necessarily and became soldiers, and therefore had all the characteristics of being a conscripted army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: They were disciplined.

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT
utterances.text: Oh, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, just to clarify the point that His Honour Judge Riad has raised, are you aware that up until the breakup of the former Yugoslavia, there was a requirement for males to perform compulsory military service in the JNA?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT
utterances.text: Very much so, and that underpinned the whole defensive philosophy of the former Yugoslavia as a national policy to maintain its own independence. Widespread conscription for military service was common to make sure that All Peoples' Defence, which was their defensive doctrine, could be facilitated by widespread military training. Therefore, a return into the army of the VRS would have, perhaps, not been as much of a surprise for individuals living in that part of the world than it would be, let's say, in Great Britain.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So indeed in 1991, most males over the age of 18 who served in the VRS would have completed some form of military service in the JNA?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT
utterances.text: A high proportion would have done, assuming they were fit and weren't in a small number of occupations that excluded them from military service.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, General, just briefly going back to your time in the former Yugoslavia, can you give to the Judges very briefly your opinion regarding the Bosnian Serb army, what you saw when you arrived in country in 1994, 1995?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT
utterances.text: My direct exposure to the Bosnian Serb army, the VRS, really did not start until we began to implement the Dayton Peace Agreement in December 1995. As the majority of UN soldiers were located and based within the area controlled by the Muslims and the Croats, and indeed in my own case that is exactly where I was, my contact with the VRS only began rather as I described a little earlier in my dealings, my attempt to deal with General Talic and explain my plan. Thereafter, I had regular dealings with the VRS as we worked with them and the other two armies to implement the terms of the peace agreement. The impression I gained in December 1995 was of an army which had a coherent structure. It was an army that had been fighting hard for a number of years, and certainly in Western Bosnia, which was where my experience directly was, it was a very tired army that in many ways, I wouldn't say it was a defeated army, but it had taken a number of hard knocks during the course of autumn 1995 in the face of a sustained attack by Croat and Muslim forces in an operation known as Operation Storm. And therefore the forces around Banja Luka were certainly tired, and while coherent and had a command structure that was in place, definitely in need of a rest. One of the problems that the Bosnia Serb army had throughout the war, because it had retained most of the former JNA's equipment, tanks and artillery and heavy equipment, they were quite strong, but they were always short of manpower. And I think this was one of the major constraining factors. By contrast, the Muslim army had little equipment certainly early on but quite a lot of manpower, but the VRS always seemed to be short of manpower, and this was quite a constraint upon them. I'm going on too far. To my mind, the operations in mid-summer 1995 were to reduce the enclaves of Srebrenica and Zepa, and it might have been Gorazde as well, were probably in part conducted with the intention of having to remove the necessity to guard those two enclaves and free more soldiers to take part in operations elsewhere. It goes back to the point about shortage of manpower because I think at that stage the High Command of the VRS knew that the large Muslim-Croat offensive was coming in the west, and therefore to reduce their responsibilities and liabilities in the east of the country would have allowed more manpower to be redeployed around to the west, and indeed in autumn 1995, one saw that operation come in, in very strong terms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, let's move swiftly on to the next part of your report which addresses the command and control. You've titled it "Responsibilities, The Roles and Responsibilities of a Corps Commander and Chief of Staff Generally," and then with specific reference to the Drina Corps. Now, you yourself had been a Chief of Staff in a British Army brigade; you currently have a Chief of Staff who is a full colonel in your division. Can you explain to the Judges on universal principles the role of a Chief of Staff within -- at your level within a division, based on your experience within a brigade?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT
utterances.text: The overall division of responsibilities between a Commander and his Chief of Staff are that the Commander exercises personal overall authority and takes personal responsibility for all those under his command. He commands in the fullest sense of that word "command." The Chief of Staff assists the Commander to exercise his command by controlling the activities of the command, of the corps, of the division, of the brigade, and coordinating all the activities of the subordinates. When one talks about a command and control process, the Commander is actually carrying out the command function; the Chief of Staff is essentially carrying out the control and coordination function. That is certainly how I operated as a brigade Chief of Staff in the mid-1980's and how I expected my Chief of Staff when I was a Brigade Commander to act in my support, and how I expect my current Chief of Staff to act in support of my current functions. Indeed, today, for example, I am here; my Chief of Staff is at my headquarters. If an issue arose and an urgent decision was needed I would have perfect confidence in him to make that decision because he knows me well enough to know how I would react in the circumstances. If, however, it was very, very important, I expect him to get on the phone to me here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On page 13 of your report, you state that even though others may be of similar rank to him, to the Commander, he is primus inter pares, effectively, the most senior. Can you explain what you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT
utterances.text: Yes, I can. And I'm talking obviously about the command and control system that I am most familiar with which is my own British command and control system, and that is that within the headquarters, my current headquarters, my Chief of Staff is a full colonel. There are five other full colonels in that headquarters. They are of equal rank, but because he holds the appointment of Chief of Staff, they know he is the senior amongst those, although they are all of the same rank. Because he's the Chief of Staff, he holds the senior appointment; hence, he's the first amongst equals. And that system works both at the brigade level, divisional level, and at the corps level.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, General, you have looked at various documents that we've provided to you in respect of the general regulations of the JNA. Indeed, we provided to you the JNA 4th Corps Regulations and the JNA Regulations of the Land Army Corps Peacetime.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Those, Your Honours, are Prosecutor's Exhibit 402, tab 3/7 and Prosecutor's Exhibit 410.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I won't place them in front of you, but from your study of those particular documents, how do you find the role of a Chief of Staff in a corps in the VRS?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT
utterances.text: The role of a Chief of Staff within the VRS in many ways is similar to the role of a Chief of Staff that I'm familiar with and in which capacity I have acted, with one principal exception, and perhaps I should deal with that exception straight away. From my study of the JNA/VRS regulations, the Chief of Staff also holds the appointment, the dual appointment of Deputy Commander; and therefore, in the absence of the Commander, either on duty on or leave, or whether it be as a result of being a casualty, the Chief of Staff by regulation becomes the Commander. This is not the case in the system that the British Army follows in that another officer is appointed as the Deputy Commander and the person who would take over command if the Commander became a casualty. However, the Chief of Staff still in those circumstances where the Commander has become a casualty, the Chief of Staff still exercises command for a short period of time until a new Commander is appointed. So that is the one difference that by regulation in the JNA/VRS, the Chief of Staff is also the Deputy Commander, certainly at corps level. Otherwise, I see very many similarities in the way that I have operated as a Chief of Staff and in the way the JNA/VRS regulations require one of their Chiefs of Staff to operate. And the success of a Chief of Staff is in many ways measured by the quality of his relationship with his Commander. If he understands his Commander well and they get on well together and understand and work well as a team, then the Chief of Staff is likely to be a pretty effective Chief of Staff. Where there is a bad relationship, it's not very successful, and indeed, it's probably better for all parties if the Commander finds a new Chief of Staff fairly rapidly rather than have somebody he can't get on with.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you state in paragraph 38 of your report that the role of the Chief of Staff within the VRS is a privileged and onerous position that puts the Chief of Staff far closer in relationship and responsibility to the Commander than any other staff officer or subordinate Commander. Can you expand on that statement at all?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT
utterances.text: Yes. I think for both the two reasons that I've already given, first, the Chief of Staff is a first amongst equals; and second, because he has to exercise command in the Commander's absence, then he has to know as much of what is going on as the Commander does. He has to orchestrate on behalf of the Commander the workings of all the staff in the headquarters, and he is very much the focal point of making everything happen. And it therefore takes a very special and qualified and well-trained person to do that and to do it effectively because he is the principal mechanism by which the Commander can get his intentions, his actions carried out throughout his command, and therefore it's a very responsible and onerous position. There must be this level of trust between the Commander and his Chief of Staff so that what the Commander wants actually is delivered through the actions of the Chief of Staff coordinating and controlling the activities of all the headquarters and coordinating the work of the superior subordinate Commanders and their commands.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, let us move on to Corps or Divisional Commander. You are a Major General. You command a division of the British Army; you've already described to the Judges the military unit that you command. Now, in your report, you state, and I'll read it word for word: "Command is a personal matter in the sense that the Commander takes personal responsibility for all that goes on and is done by all those under his command." Now, that statement does speak for it itself, but could you explain exactly what you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT
utterances.text: Command is a personal thing in that every Commander is given orders himself from above and he is responsible for carrying out those orders and achieving the mission, achieving the intent of his superior; therefore, in that sense he is personally liable for the success or failure of the actions of all those under his command. That, then, flows down in that he must ensure that all those under his command are doing what he wants done in the way that he wants done in the manner that he has laid down and to the timings to create the effect that he wants to do. If something goes wrong, then he has to take responsibility in a personal way for it. Throughout military history, one has seen senior commanders removed from their posts after a reverse, and this is usually as a result of mistakes made or some bad decision made and someone has to take personal responsibility and personal liability for it. A senior commander may be removed from post and someone else put in place. That is when the personal accountability and the personal nature of command really is at its sharpest and has seen greatest effect.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that principle unique to the British Army?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT
utterances.text: No, it's not. One's seen that throughout many armies in the world: that when an operation or campaign is successful, the successful General will be given various medals or awards or whatever, but when there is failure, at least personal failure, then he's removed. One can see that probably through, I hesitate to say, every army, but the majority of armies throughout military history. Where it's gone well, the General has been congratulated; where it's gone badly, he's often been removed. It's a personal thing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I can't put my finger on it in the report, but you do discuss the amount of time that various -- these different sides of military units take to plan operations. To give the gist of what you say: The higher level of command, the larger the formation, the longer the planning period; the smaller the formation, the less the planning period. Can you explain that to the Judges?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT
utterances.text: Yes. I've already explained that a division in my army, for example, is made up of a number of brigades and a corps in my army is made up of a number of divisions. These aren't just sort of a hierarchial amalgam of smaller formations but an indication that at each level there's a different function to be carried out. Essentially, battalions and brigades at the lower level are fighting current battles at the tactical level, whereas above them a divisional headquarters will be planning a subsequent operation, probably 48 to 72 hours, two to three days, ahead. They will also at the same time be monitoring what is also going on in their area, the brigades and battalions fighting the current battle, but at the same time they are planning the future operation, as I say, 48 to 72 hours out. The same thing is happening at the level above them. At the corps headquarters level, again they are monitoring the divisions and brigades fighting the current battle but they're also planning even further out, probably 96, four days; shaping the battle's future intentions. After all, we're talking about large bodies of people, large amounts of movement to be ordered, and therefore people have got to have a sufficiently long lead time to make sure that everything is organised. So the higher the level, the further out the planning is. Typically, four days at corps level; two to three days at divisional level; and at brigade level, it's all within a 24-hour time frame, a one-day time frame.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, here, General, you're talking about the British Army/NATO structures. But does this principle apply again universally, the principle of longer periods of planning for larger formations. The time periods may be different, of course.

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT
utterances.text: It does apply universally. It has to apply universally, just because the logical thinking through of the process, you can't get a force of 15.000 to 20.000 men to do something just at the flick of a switch; it takes a period of time to plan it. People have to have responsibility to think ahead, to plan ahead, and therefore by logical definition or logical deduction, a higher headquarters has to be thinking further ahead. That is a universal principle for all armies. They could not operate if that was not the case. The only time -- the only time -- that an army or the higher headquarters are not planning ahead, frankly, is when they're on the back foot, when they're under pressure, and they're probably losing in a particular operation. When you're planning in a hurry, you're probably not planning very well and you're probably not far off being defeated.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's move on to the manner in which you, as a divisional commander, make decisions. On what do you base decisions that you make in your division?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT
utterances.text: I base the decisions that I make on a number of things. First of all, I will base it on advice that I'm given by my staff, and by "my staff," I'm referring to a whole variety of functions within the staff: the intelligence staff, the operations staff, logistics staff, personnel staff. There are a whole range of staff functions all of whom will provide me advice; principally provide me advice on the intelligence and operations side through the Chief of Staff and on the personnel and logistics side through the Deputy Chief of Staff. So the staff is one major input. Secondly, the reports and opinions and assessments of my subordinate commanders, how they read the situation, how they read the battle. I'm very interested to hear their views. And then thirdly, I overlay my own military education, my own experience, and my own judgement on that and I will then make my decision.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On operations, are you briefed regularly by your staff?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT
utterances.text: Yes, I am. When I'm in my main headquarters, which is not the whole time, I'm briefed twice a day formally. Our sequence of events is to do this at 8.00 in the morning and 8.00 at night, when all the principal staff officers gather around the operations table and, to a set sequence, they update me on what is going on in their areas of responsibility by staff function, and also across the geographical area that I might be responsible for at that particular time. That is a comprehensive and a formal briefing which we do, as I say, twice a day, at 8.00 in the morning and at 8.00 in the evening. Now, at other times, I can ask for additional reports, or, indeed, if a subordinate commander has got something important that he wants to tell me, he will get in touch at any time or, indeed, if there's a particular question that I want to ask him, at any time I could ask him. So there is a formal regular process which is supplemented by other dialogue as necessary.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you state in your report that you regard it as a major part of your responsibility to be out and about talking to commanders and soldiers within your division; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT
utterances.text: It is. One of the major tricks in being a successful commander is to know where to be at the right moment. Probably in the planning stage of an operation, the commander should be in his main headquarters where most of the staff are because that is where most of the information is. The information can be assessed, converted into a plan, and that is, therefore, by definition, the correct place for him to be. But when an operation is ongoing, when one's involved in a battle, then quite probably the best place for the commander to be is away from his headquarters, possibly in the area where most activity is going on. He might wish to go to the busiest area to speak with the subordinate commander in that area, to get his assessment, to get a feel for what is going on on the ground, so that he can overlay on his knowledge of the overall situation and his knowledge of the plan, and here I'm referring to the Commander, the assessment of the subordinate commander in that area. Again, the Germans once again have a very good term for this, they call it fingerspitzengefuhl, fingertip control; the commander having a good feel for what is going on, such as the sensitivity at the end of the fingers, so that he can make the right decision based on the right information at the time. So the commander has to decide where he should be at any one time, whether it's in the main headquarters, whether it's in his forward tactical headquarters, or whether it's visiting one of his units either to give them encouragement or to find out for himself what action is going on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, General, although the specifics may differ from army to army, again what you've just said, is this a universal principle of command throughout the world?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT
utterances.text: Yes, it is. I can't really countenance a well-trained, well-structured army whereby a Commander could really operate in a different way. In a sense, technology these days is driving Commanders to spend more time in their main headquarters because technology can make the information so good. But I would suggest that a Commander, even because the information was so good he stayed in his main headquarters the whole time, is going to become a less effective Commander pretty quickly. He must get out and about and get a feel for what is going on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, moving on to the Bosnian Serb army -- again, you viewed the regulations which I won't show you -- based on your review of these documents, can you explain to the Judges how you see the role of General Krstic as the Commander of the Drina Corps?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT
utterances.text: I would see him operating in pretty much the way that I've just been describing. My understanding of the way that the Drina Corps was constructed, it's similar to my division in that there is a main headquarters where for most of the time I would expect to see most of the staff. There is also a forward headquarters, a tactical headquarters, to which, as a Commander, either I or General Krstic would deploy to for a particular period to oversee a given operation. Again, it comes back to what I was just saying. Part of the art of command, and we teach at the Staff College that it is an art rather than a science, is to know where to be when; when to be in the forward headquarters, the tactical headquarters, and when to be back in the main headquarters or when to be elsewhere. My understanding of the sequence of events and the history in the period that we're talking about is that General Krstic at some time was in his main headquarters and at some times was in a forward headquarters, and that's what I would expect during a period such as this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in paragraph 31 of your report, at page 11, and I'll read from the end of the first line onwards: "... the Corps Commander is fully, and personally, accountable for the conduct of all military operations in the Corps zone of responsibility. Furthermore he is specifically charged to ensure that there is an uninterrupted flow of information and situation reports into and out of his Headquarters. In short, he is required to stay in touch with his superiors and all his subordinates, at all times." On what do you base these two statements?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT
utterances.text: I base that statement having looked through a number of the regulations pertaining to the former JNA 4th Corps, which, to my understanding, became the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps in the VRS and as such is most probably typical of the way that all the corps of the VRS operated. I've not seen the regulations for the Drina Corps; I don't believe they are in the possession of yourselves, or certainly I haven't seen them.
