But I have no reason to believe that what I've seen in the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps would be any different from the way the Drina Corps operated. Under the regulations that I have looked at, the basic duties of the Commander are laid down. They're quite specific. When you aggregate those specific responsibilities together, I can make the statement that you have just quoted. I don't know whether you want me to go through, for the information of the Court, what those basic duties are, but I do have them listed in front of me if that would be of assistance.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think they're clearly contained, actually, on page 10 and 11 of your report so I don't think there's a necessity to go through each and every one, although, indeed, the Defence may have some questions for you about this. We'll just come back to this in more detail later in your testimony, but you have certainly reviewed reports available to the Prosecutor which are going into the Drina Corps from subordinate brigades, and in reviewing those documents, what is your opinion on the reporting procedure within the Drina Corps, at least as far as the brigades were concerned?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT
utterances.text: I've seen a number of documents originating from several of the subordinate brigades which are daily combat reports, reporting activity going on in their brigade areas to the corps level of command. Those daily combat reports follow a set pattern, a set format, and they are broadly common to all those brigades. So what that says to me is that there were orders and regulations laid down within the corps which told the subordinate formations, the brigades, when they had to report, and what they had to report, and the manner in which they had to report. These appeared to be coming through on a daily basis. Indeed, they are called "daily combat reports"; therefore, by definition they appear to be every 24 hours. And indeed, in the operation order that I've seen for the operation for the attack on Zepa, it is laid down that all the brigades will report their situation at 1700 hours each day, and that report to be at the corps level of command by 1800 hours that day. And what that says to me, we've got a well organised and efficient military formation here, which is what I would expect to see, given that one of the basic duties of the Corps Commander and the regulations I was just referring to, I'm now quoting, "Is to make sure there is uninterrupted contact with the Superior Command as well as with the subordinate and attached commands and units." It was laid down that this regular flow of information would happen. Indeed, the reports I've seen indicate that it did happen and was happening at the time in question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To move to a specific area of command before we move on to the third and final part of your report, are you aware who the Assistant Commander for security was within the Drina Corps?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT
utterances.text: Yes. We're talking about Colonel Popovic?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's correct, General. Now, do you have a similarly appointed officer on your staff who is responsible for security matters within your division?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT
utterances.text: Within my division, the intelligence and security function is delivered by a Major who is answerable to my Chief of Staff upwards within the staff hierarchy and downwards. This Major has two Captains who work for him, one of whom is specifically responsible for security and with a small staff to help him, and another who is responsible for intelligence and, again, with a small staff to support him.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If, Mr. Usher, you could give to the witness Prosecutor's Exhibit 418.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, General, if you could look particularly at paragraph 16 and 18, you've looked at all of this document, and the simple question for you is this: Within whose chain of command did Colonel Popovic fall within the VRS? Under whose command did he fall?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT
utterances.text: Colonel Popovic as a member of the staff of the Drina Corps was under the command of the Commander of the Drina Corps. There is no doubt about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What relationship did Colonel Popovic have with the Main Staff security officer?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT
utterances.text: Ah, well, that's a different issue, and I recognise the same kind of system within my own army, that at the level above whatever level one is at, there are going to be people in the higher headquarters who also are carrying out the similar functional responsibilities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, could I interrupt you? Because I'll give you Prosecutor's Exhibit 398. You've actually come on to the point.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So if the witness could be given 398, which is, I'll say this for the benefit of Their Honours, is a diagram in fact indicating the structure. I have it here, Mr. Usher. I have a copy if you don't have it available, and if it could be placed under the camera. If the technical booth could focus down.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, General, you'll have to read this, it's going to be upside down for you, but --

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT
utterances.text: That's all right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, this is specifically your organisation. Whereabouts is your command, if you could point to it on the exhibit?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT
utterances.text: Currently, that's my position there as Divisional Commander.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And above you in --

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT
utterances.text: In a full NATO deployment sense, that would be a corps, a Corps Commander at the Corps Command level.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And he would be a Lieutenant General?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT
utterances.text: He would indeed, yeah.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, under your division you've put "Chief of Staff" and "G2."

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT
utterances.text: Yes, if I could just explain this. It's really what I was saying a moment or two ago. Under the Chief of Staff there are a number of staff branches. G2, it's the NATO nomenclature for the intelligence and security staff, and in my headquarters, that post is filled by a Major, and beneath him he has a Captain responsible for security, and he has another Captain responsible for intelligence. Up here I could be showing a whole series of other boxes of G1 to G9 as it happens, but I think we're just talking about intelligence and security now. But the security Captain is answerable to the Major, who is answerable to the Chief of Staff above him, who is answerable to me. But I think the question you were asking me before is, what is the relationship between the Divisional Command and the Corps Command as far as the security function is concerned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I could just ask you one question to make things absolutely clear. The Corps Command within the NATO structure, the Corps Commander also has a Chief of Staff and also has a G2 branch and also has a security branch?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT
utterances.text: Indeed, the functions are mirrored at the levels above. Now, the way that it operates is that the security staff, and it could be the personnel staff, the operations staff, any of the other staffs, obviously need to do business on a day-to-day basis with the equivalent staff at the level above. After all, information is always going to be more comprehensive, probably better, at the higher level. So if the man on my staff responsible for, we'll say, security wants to ask security questions that he does not have the answers to, the logical and first place that he would go to would be to go to the security staff at the level above him. I'm at division level. He would therefore go to the corps level, and the security staff there would be perfectly in order for there to be a dialogue between the security staff at my headquarters and the security staff at the higher headquarters. And that's why on this diagram, I don't know whether you can see it, I've shown a dotted line there, this sort of line of liaison and dialogue. But that's very different from the solid line which actually is the command line. The security staff are linked to me by the solid line. I am linked to the Corps Commander by a solid line, but down here it's a dotted line indicating liaison, dialogue, discussion, but it's not a command line. And, well, in my organisation I would get extremely shirty if I found that someone on my staff was taking orders from someone on the staff elsewhere. We don't operate like that. Sorry, shirty is -- I'll get cross.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you've read the VRS regulations on the security organ. You've reviewed a large number of documents and, indeed, some intercepts. What was the relationship between Lieutenant Colonel Popovic and General Krstic when General Krstic was the Commander of the Drina Corps?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT
utterances.text: From some of the material that I've seen, it's -- I describe it as a normal relationship. Colonel Popovic commands or heads one of the staff functions within the Drina Corps headquarters and staff, and I see a certain amount of dialogue, questions being asked, both upwards and downwards. Between General Krstic and Colonel Popovic, in the same way that I might quiz any of the heads of branch of my own staff seeking clarification on certain issues or giving direction on certain issues.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What would have been Lieutenant Colonel Popovic's relationship with the security organ on the Main Staff of the VRS? I don't want you to repeat everything you've said, but ...

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT
utterances.text: It would have been a relationship seeking advice, seeking the answers to questions, probably ensuring that what was going on within the Drina Corps area of responsibility in sort of security functional terms was consistent with what was going on at the higher level, making sure that there was property integration and harmony with the functionings at the higher level and the functions at the lower level. That is the nature and the purpose of the kind of dialogue that one would expect to see going on, and it's perfectly normal to go on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was Colonel Beara Lieutenant Colonel Popovic's Commander?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT
utterances.text: No. My understanding of Colonel Beara is that he has a security function and role on the Main Staff, and therefore in the way that I've been describing, would naturally have a dialogue because of a common function that they both deliver, mainly security, with Colonel Popovic. But in terms of giving orders to, I don't recognise that at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If the witness could be given Exhibit 622 and 661.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Mr. Cayley, your question was, was Colonel Beara --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: You said, "Was Colonel Beara Lieutenant Popovic's Commander?" Popovic was a Lieutenant or Lieutenant Colonel?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Lieutenant Colonel, Judge Riad. I'm sorry if I misspoke.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: So a Lieutenant Colonel. Were they the same grade? That's the point.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Perhaps I should let the witness answer the question.

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT
utterances.text: Popovic was a Lieutenant Colonel, and I'm trying very hard to remember whether Beara was Lieutenant Colonel or a Colonel. The point that I was making, though, was that I don't recognise Popovic of whatever rank as being the subordinate of Beara of whatever rank.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, these are two intercepts. There are others.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Mr. Cayley. Microphone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, these are two intercepts. There are others that you've reviewed, but could you just briefly explain to the Judges what these represent to you, these two particular exhibits?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT
utterances.text: The first one, the larger one I'm looking at --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which is 622 for the purposes of the record.

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT
utterances.text: -- is Colonel Popovic asking to be connected with General Krstic at Zlatar, and Zlatar I understand as being the code name for the Drina Corps headquarters. He was told that General Krstic wasn't there, so he asked to be connected with someone else. And I see in the transcript of this conversation reference to the fact of reports, being an interim report, and really it's Colonel Popovic trying to pass a report to his Commander, to General Krstic, that particular actions that were ongoing at the time had been finished. In fact, he says, "I'll come there tomorrow, so tell the General I've finished the job." So there was obviously something that Colonel Popovic had been tasked to do, and he felt a responsibility to tell General Krstic that whatever it was had been done. And that's normal, and I would expect a subordinate member of staff to want to inform his General that this indeed was the case. And the other one is similar. We have a conversation here, and I see, for example, that it says find this Popovic chap and have him report to the forward command post. So Colonel Popovic had gone missing for a bit but was uncontactable, and it was deemed important for him to get in touch with the command post where, I would presume, General Krstic was so that he could either deliver or clarify his report or, indeed, receive further instructions. So I see evidence here of a very normal superior/subordinate relationship going on, which is what I would expect.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. Usher. If I could have that exhibit back because that's the Prosecutor's copy. Thank you. Mr. President, I don't know whether the Judges wish to ask any questions on this area at this time, or if you wish me to move to the final part of General Dannatt's report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Cayley, I think it would be convenient to have a break because General Krstic needs to move because of his leg, so perhaps we can have a 15-minute break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Cayley, let us continue, bearing in mind that around a quarter to two we will have another break.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, if we could move on to the final and fullest part of your evidence which is command and control operations: the operational and logistic planning, tactical tempo, headquarters command and control procedures relevant to this case, and that begins on page 13 of your report. Now, you should have Prosecutor's Exhibit 425 in front of you and this is a document that you've seen. This is a document from the Supreme Command of the armed forces of Republika Srpska. It's from the ... General, you've looked at this document. Specifically, I'd like you to go to page 10 which is the direction to the Drina Corps in respect of what was to happen to the enclaves in Srebrenica and Zepa. Now, looking at that entire section, and particularly drawing your attention to the following words: "By planned and well-thought-out combat operations create an unbearable situation of total insecurity with no hope of further survival or life for the inhabitants of Srebrenica and Zepa," what kind of direction is this, General?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT
utterances.text: It's a slightly puzzling directive, or part of the directive in that it's not, to me as a military person, entirely clear what it is that the political authorities actually want. My first inclination, I have to say, would probably be to go back and try and seek a dialogue with the originator of this to try and get more specific about what it is that they wanted me to do. When I read the words "By planned and well-thought-out combat operations to create an unbearable situation of total insecurity with no hope of further survival or life for the inhabitants of Srebrenica and Zepa," it's pretty broad and it's pretty ambiguous, and as a military person, I wouldn't be very comfortable with that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, bearing in mind that you've said it's broad, that you would go back for clarification, what kind of operation is envisaged by this particular plan?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT
utterances.text: Well, I think what is intended here is that Srebrenica and Zepa should be captured. I would assume that the reference to "no hope of further survival or life for the inhabitants of Srebrenica and Zepa" meant that not only were those towns to be captured but that the existing population should be removed from those places. Given, I think, my earlier comment that manpower was at a premium, manpower was in short supply as far as the Bosnian Serb army is concerned, if there wasn't a Muslim enclave in Srebrenica or wasn't a Muslim enclave in Zepa and therefore there were no Muslim military elements there, then there would be no requirement to have manned confrontation lines around those two enclaves, and therefore it would be a considerable saving of manpower and resources for the Bosnian Serb army. So from my point of view, I would therefore understand it as being a sensible military operation to take place, what I would call an economy-of-effort operation, so that manpower could be diverted away from this area and put to where, perhaps, it was going to be more needed. As I've already suggested, there was strong indications and strong intelligence that there was going to be a sizable attack mounted in the west of Bosnia, and therefore the more deployable reserve elements could be taken away from the eastern area and sent round to the Banja Luka, Mrkonjic Grad, Prijedor, Sanski Most sort of areas in the west. A complete reduction of Srebrenica and Zepa, I think, is what is required here.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If the witness could be shown Prosecutor's Exhibit 427 and 428.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, General, this is the preparatory order and the combat order for Krivaja 95, the taking of the Srebrenica enclave. From a pure military format point of view, is this what you would expect to see, a preparatory order and a combat order? If so, can you explain the difference between these two orders?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT
utterances.text: Yes, the normal convention in planning a military operation is to issue initially a warning order to give advance notification to those units that might be required to take part in an operation, to give them an outline of what they're likely to have to do and when so that battle procedure, as it's termed in the military, getting things going, can begin. And then the main document is what I would recognise as being an operation order issued by the Drina Corps for a significant operation, and it gives, as I would expect, missions to subordinate commands and coordinates the other activity necessary to ensure successful delivery of an operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: For the purposes of the record, 427 is the warning or preparatory order; 428 is the main combat order.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I don't want to go through the whole of this combat order, but if you could go to page 3, General, and place that on the ELMO next to you. First of all, paragraph 2 states: "The Command of the Drina Corps, pursuant to Operations Directive no. 7 and 7/1 of the [GS] VRS /Main Staff ..." et cetera. Now, you would agree with me that this paragraph is referring back to the document that we've just referred to, the document signed by President Karadzic, Prosecutor's Exhibit 425; would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT
utterances.text: Yes, that is the document referred to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, in essence, the military operation envisaged and, indeed, incorporated the planning and the political direction contained in Exhibit 425 for the elimination of the enclave and for the removal of the civilian population; would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT
utterances.text: Yes, I would. It is perfectly normal at the start of an operation order to review the situation, but also to review the higher orders that have been issued that authorise, if you like, the operation that is about to be described in the main body of the operation order. It provides the context, and as far as subordinate Commanders are concerned, shows them the authority under which the operation is being planned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And would the document signed by President Karadzic have been referred to by senior officers in deciding what was the ultimate aim of this operation, Krivaja-95?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT
utterances.text: I can see no reason why it shouldn't be. It's perfectly reasonable to be done so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you could now go to page 5 of that document, and I want you to specifically address the paragraph which is -- you can see it's in the middle of the screen, "Reserve Forces." What can you say about that particular paragraph, General?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT
utterances.text: I think I've got two comments, really. One is in the sequence which has been followed through in this order and the sequence up to this point here, has shown particular tasks and missions being assigned to a number of the subordinate brigades. That's already gone before. Then we get to this piece here which talks about reserves, and in general military convention, the subordinate commands that are part of a higher command have their missions shown first and in order. In this case it's the brigades, and after the brigades have been given their tasks, we then get quite naturally to the task of the reserve forces. So I'm reading a mission about reserve forces at the correct place in the sequence where by normal military convention, I would expect to find it. And interestingly enough, after it -- or interesting to me, anyway, I believe that I see orders being given to the artillery, and that is what I would expect in the normal convention logically to come after the reserve. So my first comment is that this instruction for reserve forces comes in the correct place in a good operation order. My second comment is looking at that reserve force, it's a small reserve force, two or three companies of Ministry of Interior Police troops and one company of the Vlasenica Light Infantry Brigade, so we've got three or four companies. I don't know how many men that would necessarily have been at that time, but we're talking between 100 and 200. It might have been a bit more. That sort of size force. Quite a handy force for a Superior Commander to have kept as a genuine reserve to deal with unexpected situations. And in military planning, a reserve force is exactly that. It's a force kept as a genuine hedge against the unexpected to deal with the unexpected situation. Not one that's assigned a task at this stage, it can react to whatever needs to be done. And it's interesting here that Drina Corps is giving orders to a company of one of its own brigades, the Vlasenica Brigade, but also giving orders to two or three companies of Ministry of Interior Police which by the regulations for combat operations, those Ministry of Interior police companies would come under command of the army and of the Drina Corps in these situations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I could just show you, General, two intercepts which you've looked at, Prosecutor's Exhibit 504 and Prosecutor's Exhibit 529, and I don't think you have those. The usher is just about to give them to you. And if you could in the context of speaking of the military police -- of the, I'm sorry, of the MUP, of the Ministry of Interior Police, what these particular documents show. And if you could place them on the ELMO, that would be helpful. This is Prosecutor's Exhibit 504. What can you say about this particular document, General?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT
utterances.text: What that says to me is rather consistent with what I was just saying about the operation order, that we have a military police unit within the Drina Corps task organisation and force structure for this operation that is clearly part of the command and control structure and quite happy to accept and receive orders from the Drina Corps command. As it says here, so that he can give orders to them through the Commander of the Engineering Battalion. This is a means of command and control that's been establish to pass messages to that police organisation through the engineering battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And this date of this intercept, Your Honours, is in fact the 12th of July. If we could move to the next intercept, General, and this is between the accused, General Krstic, and, as you know already, Borovcanin who was the Deputy Commander for the MUP Brigade. What does this conversation demonstrate to you?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT
utterances.text: It demonstrates really the same thing, that there is an established command relationship between General Krstic and this police Commander, and they're discussing the operation. And there are aspects of the operation being talked about in exactly the same way that I would expect within a superior/subordinate command relationship, asking for information and giving it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, General, you mentioned earlier that you'd actually reviewed the regulations which is Prosecutor's Exhibit 420 -- I won't show them to you now; the Defence may well wish to show them to you -- but do you see anything within that particular document that would be inconsistent with your conclusion that these MUP units were under the Corps Command at the relevant time? You have it in front of you now. It's Article 14.

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT
utterances.text: There is one aspect to it, and that's in the third paragraph of Article 14: "Police units resubordinated to the army of Republika Srpska in a certain zone shall be used only for combat operations established in advance by the Commander-in-Chief or the Minister of the Interior." And that would indicate to me that it's only legitimate for the Drina Corps in this set of circumstances to have used those MUP companies while there was combat ongoing. That said, what we in fact saw happening on the ground in that period in July indicated that combat operations were ongoing for really quite some time, and particularly the combat operations against the Muslim column particularly made up of 28th Division breaking out of Srebrenica. That posed a major threat to the security of the Drina Corps, and I would have thought that operations against that column was undoubtedly combat operations and were the sort of operations that would be particularly well suited to those MUP companies' characteristics and capabilities being involved, and there were certainly combat operations. Therefore, whereas perhaps one might have thought that they stopped being available to the Drina Corps after the attack on Srebrenica was concluded, it would seem to me that combat continued for quite some time against that column, and therefore I presume that those Ministry of Interior Police remained under the command of the Drina Corps until that column had been dealt with, which I understand from reading other things took really quite some time, well into July, latter part of July.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If we could briefly return to Prosecutor's Exhibit 428, and I wanted to review one more section within this -- actually, two more sections. On page 7 of the English translation, there is a direction, "In dealing with prisoners of war and the civilian population, behave in every way in accordance with the Geneva Conventions." General, is that the kind of direction that you would give in one of your orders to your brigades, and what would you mean by that if you said that?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT
utterances.text: It's the kind of statement that actually I wouldn't think it was necessary to place in an OP order. I would like it to be thought to be implicit in anything that I in my division would order, that my soldiers would act in accordance with the Geneva Convention anyway. There are some things, as we say, are SOP, they are "standard operating procedures," and it's certainly standard to operate in accordance with the Geneva Convention. However, it is mentioned specifically here, so I would judge that for whatever reason, the originator of this order felt it was necessary to remind his people that there was an obligation to operate within the normal -- the accepted norms, within the accepted norms and standards laid down by the Geneva Convention.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you could go to the final page, page 9, and if you could place that on the ELMO. Yes, that's perfect. First of all, in paragraph 11 it refers to the IKM-1 of the Drina Corps, the IKM being the forward command post that you've referred to earlier. Is this where the battle would have been fought, in essence, in Srebrenica, where the battle would have been conducted from?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT
utterances.text: Yes. I mean, as I was saying before, an operation like this would have been planned in all probability at the main headquarters, and then the executive function, the implementation of the battle, carried out at the forward headquarters which is what is referred to here, the forward command post. And that's where I would expect the Commander to be for the majority of his time, other than when he wanted to go even further forward to visit the headquarters of one of his subordinate formations or need to go on the ground and see what was going on. That's where tactical command and control of the operation would have been mounted from.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've also spoken about the need for a Commander to keep in contact, keep in communication, with his subordinate units, and indeed there is this final paragraph of this reporting requirement. Does this reflect and reinforce what you stated earlier about the reporting procedure within the corps?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT
utterances.text: Yes. It's, again, what I would expect: submit daily reports every day until 1800 hours -- the word "until" I don't quite understand, I'm assuming there's a translation aspect to that -- with a situation report at 1700 hours. But what I understand from that, those couple of lines, is that each brigade every day should send a situation report at 1700 hours, and that those daily reports should be at the command post by 1800 hours, and interim reports as necessary should be sent in addition. And although I've referred earlier that some things are standard procedure, in an order like this, this is the sort of thing that could be repeated just so that everyone was quite clear when the daily report had to come. It was as at what time, and had to be at headquarters at what time. That's something I would expect to see in a decent OP order.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, this order is signed by the Commander, General Zivanovic. Who would have been responsible for drafting this combat order?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT
utterances.text: A large combat order like this would have been worked on for a period of time beforehand, a day or two or maybe longer beforehand, by various members of the staff, coordinated by the Chief of Staff, and he would have overseen the overall drafting of it; and then when he was content that the order was complete, properly described what the Commander wanted, he would then have shown it to the Commander and invited him to sign it. And I understand that General Zivanovic did indeed sign this order. That said, it's not unusual, certainly in my army, for the Chief of Staff to sign such an order on behalf of the Commander, and it comes back to this point that there is this special relationship between the Chief of Staff and the Commander, and indeed, the Chief of Staff in many ways carries the authority that the Commander does. But here, General Zivanovic himself has signed it as the Commander. He wouldn't have written it; the staff would have written it under the direction of the Chief of Staff.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, General. We'll move on now. I have shown to you a video of events in and around Bravo Company in Srebrenica on the 9th, 10th of July, 1995. That is an exhibit; it's in evidence. The Defence have a copy of it. And I've also shown to you some of the testimony of professional officers from the Dutch Battalion who were present there at the time, in and around Bravo Company or at the operations centre in Potocari, receiving reports about what was happening in Srebrenica. There's a large amount of testimony about this. I'm only going to select three, and I'll read some very brief extracts. I've already shown you this. This first extract is from the Deputy Commander of the Dutch Battalion, Major Robert Franken, and this is what he said about what was happening in Srebrenica. He was at the operations centre. He was receiving reports from his company, from the battalion's company in Srebrenica. He said to my question: "Q. From your recollection, thinking back now to July of 1995, do you have any recollection of the number of shells that fell on the city that day?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that I ordered Bravo Company to start reporting every single explosion, and it was -- when we reached the figure of about 200.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you stated in an earlier response that there was no military objective by this stage that would require this level of firing, and I'll ask you the question again: In your opinion, what was the reason for this very heavy shelling?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT
utterances.text: There could have been two reasons, but was the same effect: killing people or trying to raise a panic by killing people. And I mean by 'people,' I mean civilians, women and children."

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And that can be found, for the purposes of the Defence and the Court, at page 2019 of the transcript, lines 3 to 17.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: (redacted)

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "A. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: (redacted)

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT
utterances.text: (redacted)

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: (redacted)

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT
utterances.text: (redacted)

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT
utterances.text: This is the last section. This is an individual called Captain Egbers. He was a Captain when he testified here. He was a Platoon Commander in Srebrenica. A young officer present at a blocking position. "Q. Now, you said also that you could see some tanks coming and firing.

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT
utterances.text: I could, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know the direction of their fire?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I could. They fired into the town of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there any military targets, as far as you're aware, in the town of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT
utterances.text: No, sir. Just refugees and a UN base.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have an opinion then as to the purpose of the firing of the tank rounds into the town of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT
utterances.text: I think they wanted to scare the refugees who were in the city of Srebrenica so they would go north to Potocari and they could enter the town. They were scaring them, and of course they were wounding them, killing them." General, I don't want you to comment on the reliability of that evidence, but based on the observations of three officers present in the region at the time, what conclusions would you draw about the artillery that was firing into Srebrenica on that day?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT
utterances.text: It would seem to me that the artillery that was being fired was not predominantly at military targets. My understanding by that stage is that the Muslim 28th Division had, in the main, withdrawn from Srebrenica. So there were probably not many military targets against which artillery could have usefully been aimed or objectives that could have been targeted. And therefore it would seem, and it perhaps goes right back to that earlier paragraph in the political direction that you showed me some 30, 40 minutes ago, that the use of this artillery was designed to be fairly random, was designed to create fear and probably to create the effect on the civilian population to leave the town and, in this case, head towards the other UN base around Potocari. And if the intention was not only to capture, in a military sense, Srebrenica but also to ensure that it was empty of people, then I would have thought that the indiscriminate use of -- relative indiscriminate use of artillery was a good tactic to do that. And of course you don't have to kill large numbers of people to achieve that aim. One or two shells to go off close to people to cause some injuries, I suggest, would be sufficient. Most sensible people, particularly when they're already frightened and fearful, when one or two shells land near you or close to you, will soon get the message that to go to a place of safety, in this case, in the direction of Potocari, was the sensible response to take. So it would seem to me that the use of that artillery was consistent with the original political direction that was given. It appeared to be random but, in fact, was actually -- the purpose of it was to get the civilian population to leave.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, you're a professional army officer. In your view, was that a legitimate way of doing things, the way the VRS did this? Specifically, this artillery bombardment on Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT
utterances.text: Well, again, it comes back to the issue, what was the objective? If the objective was to defeat the Muslim army in Srebrenica so that Srebrenica as a military objective could be taken, then the use of artillery against military objectives in concert with infantry and armoured attacks is a perfectly legitimate and reasonable way to conduct an operation. But if, however, the use of artillery was designed more to put fear amongst the people and get the people to leave, then I would regard that as an illegitimate use of artillery. Indeed, it is contrary to the Geneva Conventions which specifically addresses the responsibility of military Commanders to not inflict unnecessary suffering on civilians and non-combatants, and it would seem that in the circumstances that was exactly what was being done. And on that basis, to me that's unacceptable. Although, as it turned out, it was actually effective.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, let's look briefly at two exhibits, 445 and 614. Exhibit 445 is an intercept; it's identified as a conversation between General Mladic and an unidentified male person. And the statement that I'm particularly interested in is the second sentence in the middle of that document. If you could place it on the ELMO. Mladic speaking: "They've all capitulated and surrendered, and we'll evacuate them all. Those who want to and those who don't want to." Now, this is a conversation, an intercept, and this is the Chief of the Main Staff, General Mladic, speaking. What does this indicate to you about the intent of the operation to capture Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT
utterances.text: Well, this would seem to further corroborate what we've been talking about for the last few minutes, that there was a stated intention right at the beginning and at the planning stage of this operation. Not only was it the intention to capture Srebrenica as a military objection, but it was also the intention to remove the people, and indeed they've all capitulated and surrendered, so they have given up, and we'll evacuate them all, those who want to and those who don't want to. That last phrase implies that there is a potential to use a degree of coercion that even those who wanted to stay would not be given the option to stay, that they were going to go. The intention is quite clear right from the start that Srebrenica would no longer have a Muslim population.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, finally on this point, Exhibit 614, the second page of that document, this is an interim combat report from the 16th of July, the previous exhibit, the intercept, was the 12th of July. If you could place that on the ELMO so that paragraph 6 is visible. This is a document signed by Vinko Pandurevic, Lieutenant Colonel, Commander of the Zvornik Brigade. "I consider that the Krivaja 95 operation is not complete as long as a single enemy soldier or civilian remains behind the front line." What does that indicate to you about the understanding that Colonel Pandurevic had about Krivaja 95, the operation to take Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT
utterances.text: Well, the order which had been produced and signed by General Zivanovic, which we looked at earlier, was a comprehensive order. It was a clear order. It had been clearly understood by subordinate Commanders, such as the Brigade Commander here, Pandurevic, and that he did not regard the mission as being accomplished, and the operation complete, as he says here, "... as long as a single enemy soldier or civilian remains behind the front line." So this was to be a thorough and complete carrying out of the operation order as produced early. He was in no doubt about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, General, we've had General Mladic stating in a radio conversation that everybody had to go; we have a Brigade Commander from the Drina Corps stating that the operation was not complete until everybody had gone. Does that indicate to you some understanding of this plan within the chain of command?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT
utterances.text: It indicates to me quite clearly that the plan, as I've already just said, was clearly written, clearly communicated, understood by subordinate Commanders who needed to know it, and was complied with thoroughly. Whatever the rights and wrongs and whatever of this might be, it was a successful military operation in terms of being a military operation. The intent was clearly communicated and the operation was thoroughly carried out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Overall, and finally on the order, what is your view, your global view of Krivaja 95? What kind of situation were the VRS trying to create by this operation, by this order?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT
utterances.text: I think I'd just refer you back, if I may, to my earlier comment that there were obvious operational-level benefits, campaign-level benefits, for the overall VRS command and control, Higher Command level, to remove Srebrenica and Zepa as Muslim enclaves within Serb territory so that they could redeploy forces elsewhere. That was an obvious and greatly advantageous objective. Secondly, by so comprehensively and thoroughly not only defeating the Muslim army in and around the Srebrenica enclave but by ensuring the removal of the civilian population there, it would then make it a town that was then available to Serb people to live in and make the Serb part of Bosnia more comprehensive and less complicated by having Muslim pockets within their own territory. It has a double and very clear logic which, from the Serb point of view, was very advantageous.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Can I ask one question?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: General Dannatt, would that benefit to the VRS be accomplished or would it be materially diminished if everybody in Srebrenica was evacuated, both the civilians and the elements, the remaining elements of the 28th which were in the column along with the civilians? In other words, if everybody had just been pushed on or allowed to get over the border, would that have made a material difference in these objectives which you're talking about?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT
utterances.text: I think the key thing was that there would be no longer a Muslim population in Srebrenica, because if there was a Muslim population there, there was the potential for there to be fighters hidden amongst the people which could, albeit in small groups, have sallied forth, broken out as, indeed, had happened earlier in the war and made attacks on Serb villages, and therefore there would still have been a need to have kept a garrison force around the outside of the enclave, and therefore it would have denied them the advantage they were seeking to gain of not having to have soldiers doing that. I just come back to the point that I made before: that manpower was at a premium for the Serb army and for it not to have to surround these enclaves was very much in their interest.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: But then why this additional overlay which appeared, where they felt they had to separate the men and, even according to their own rationalisation, find out which ones were part of the military and not let them go through?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT
utterances.text: I think there are two aspects to that, ma'am, if I can just draw on them. I think, one, it is not an unrealistic or not an unreasonable thing to have wanted to do, to separate the men from the women initially, and if they wanted to make a serious attempt to screen the men, to establish their identities, to see who might have been, in their eyes, guilty of war crimes in the past or activities in the past. After all, it is a known fact that from the Srebrenica enclave, particularly earlier in the war, Naser Oric and others attacked Serb villages, and they may well have felt that some of those attacks were outside the norms of war and, therefore -- and they may also have known who some of these people were and therefore they might have wanted to try and identify them, believing that they had a legitimate legal case against them. So that is not entirely surprising. The fact they didn't actually really do that, I think, is surprising but perhaps it's a side issue. Secondly, to separate the men from the children doesn't altogether surprise me in that we have much evidence throughout this civil war of exchanging large numbers of prisoners, one side with another. Therefore, if, for example, General Krstic or General Mladic had had in their possession, 5.000, 6.000, 8.000, 10.000 men of military age, they might well have been able to swap them for Serb prisoners being held by the other side. So on the face of it, to separate the men from the women might have served two purposes which, in the rather unusual logic prevailing at the time, might have been justifiable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I think this is a good time to have another break, another 15-minute break, that is, until three minutes past two. [In English] Three minutes past two.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Cayley, you may continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Until 2.30, would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, finally on this area, if -- the usher has disappeared. I need you to be shown an exhibit, Prosecutor's Exhibit 404/1, tab 20. I'll find the page so that we can deal with this quickly. General, this is a debriefing report produced by the Dutch government after Srebrenica. You've seen it before. If you could quickly read paragraphs 5.14 and 5.15, and then after you've read it place it on the ELMO and then make any comments about those two particular sections.

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT
utterances.text: This is a rather unfortunate paragraph, really. What it indicates to me is that Mr. Akashi, the special representative of the Secretary-General has accepted that the situation in Srebrenica has changed, that whereas it had seemed sensible for the UN in New York to have declared a safe area around Srebrenica while it was a Muslim enclave, that now the situation on the ground had changed; that the BSA, as it's described here, the VRS, had successfully mounted a military operation to capture Srebrenica as a military objective and that therefore it was no longer in Muslim military hands; that it was quite clear that the intent of the Serbs was for the civilian people to be expelled, if you like, from Srebrenica and they were to depart for Tuzla, as it says there in about line 6 or 7. Then the intention of the UN was recognising that what had happened on the ground was a changed situation, that their efforts were now geared towards protecting the people in the best way that they could to enable them to get to the area of Tuzla in a safe way, and then subsequently to evacuate the Dutch Battalion. And as I say, it's a rather sad paragraph because it indicates that the international resolve which had set up the UN safe haven was no longer going to be successful, and the situation on the ground had changed and that, therefore, the UN's objectives were much more limited just to try and safely protect the people as they were removed to Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'll just read paragraph 5.15 which is the next paragraph: "The Battalion was," and it's referring to the Dutch Battalion, "however surprised by the speed with which the Bosnian Serb army commenced the evacuation of the refugees from Potocari to Kladanj. Unexpectedly, it turned out the Bosnian Serb army already had large numbers of buses and trucks." General, what does that indicate to you?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT
utterances.text: Well, what we now know, of course, means that this should not have been a matter of surprise. We know, we were discussing it a little earlier this morning, that part of the intention of the operation was to remove the civilian population from Srebrenica, and in order to do that, a large number of buses and trucks had been gathered together in order to quickly facilitate the removal of the people. The fact that it surprised the Dutch Battalion in itself is not surprising because they did not know what the plan was. We now know that the plan was to rapidly remove the people to behind other Muslim lines, and the fact that they were able to do it quickly was because it was planned and because large numbers of buses and trucks were gathered together, made available, and as I would expect with a military formation such as the Drina Corps, it was done efficiently, done properly, and it was done quickly. Therefore, it's no surprise that actually it happened quite quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If the witness could now be shown Prosecutor's Exhibit 404/2, tab 73, which is a report from the President of the Bosniak Presidency in Srebrenica, Osman Suljic. This is a report from a session of the Municipality Presidency held on the 9th of July.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in reading this document, General, which is addressed to Mr. Izetbegovic in Sarajevo and to the Commander of the Bosnian army, Rasim Delic, what do you interpret this particular dispatch to represent?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT
utterances.text: This, if you like, is the other side of the same issue. The President of Srebrenica municipality was getting in touch with his own national President in Sarajevo to tell him that military command had dissolved, the 28th Division was no longer able to do anything to prevent Serb forces, aggressive forces from entering the town. There was chaos and panic. He was seeking an answer as quickly as possible for a corridor to be opened for the civilian population to move as quickly as possible to a place of safety behind the main Muslim lines. So the President had already recognised what had happened on the ground and was informing his own government in Sarajevo that this was the case, and as we see it in bold at the bottom: "We need an urgent reply at the latest by 2400 hours," by midnight that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If the witness could be shown Prosecutor's Exhibit 432 and 433, we can look at these two together.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, General, there is evidence, which you've addressed this in your report, that indicates that at the time of the operation on Srebrenica, on the 9th and 10th of July, there were a number of senior officers present from the Main Staff of the Bosnian Serb army. Prosecutor's Exhibit 432 indicates that General Gvero of the Main Staff may have been present. We have no sightings of him but this document indicates that he may have been there. Prosecutor's Exhibit 433 indicates that General Mladic, Major General Zivanovic, and Major General Krstic were in the Bratunac Brigade area of responsibility. So General Mladic was present on the ground in Srebrenica at the time. There's also evidence that we've provided to you that indicates that Colonel Jankovic, also of the Main Staff, was present in and around Srebrenica at the time of these events. Do you find it odd that officers of the Main Staff were present in and around Srebrenica whilst this operation was going on?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT
utterances.text: No, I don't find it odd in the slightest. What was going on around Srebrenica at that time was the most significant military activity going on in the whole of Republika Srpska at that moment, and therefore it's entirely not surprising that General Mladic, for example, the Chief of Staff of the Main Staff should have been there to see what was going on and, indeed, to influence what was going on. If I could widen it out to a more general military point. The military often describes the most significant set of activities going on, the focus of what is going on, as the main effort, and consistent with what I was saying earlier, that a higher Commander will try and put himself at the right place at the right time in order to influence the way that an operation -- the way that a battle is going. Here around Srebrenica, as I said, the most significant activity within Republika Srpska was going on and therefore it's entirely consistent that General Mladic, the overall Commander, the Chief of the Main Staff, should come there to see what was going on and, indeed, to influence it. He was supporting the main effort. The fact that General Krstic was also there, General Zivanovic was there, that's what I would expect. They, depending on the date here in Exhibit 433 -- I suppose I should put that there -- that's the 10th of the July, what I see is General Zivanovic as the Corps Commander, General Krstic as the Corps Chief of Staff, and General Mladic all being there; the responsible Commanders in that area. It's a Drina Corps operation. It's within the Drina Corps's zone of responsibility. But it's entirely consistent that the main boss, if you like, General Mladic, should turn up because this was the main effort, to influence -- to find out what was going on and to influence events on the ground. That's exactly the sort of thing I would expect, and indeed in other operations I have done the same sort of thing myself. If you'd like me to give an example. In January/February 1996, over on the western side of Bosnia that I was responsible for, we had a situation whereby a particular village of Croat people which had been within a Serb area throughout history and throughout the war had, in fact, been liberated, the advance of the Croat army had put that Croat village into a Croat-controlled part of Bosnia. People, obviously, were delighted about that because they were back amongst their own people. When the Dayton Peace Plan and the map was unveiled, that particular village was going to be put back under Serb control. Naturally, the Croat people in that village were very depressed and very disappointed about it, and their first inclination was to leave the village and to go away. But given that they had been there throughout the war and for about 300 years, as far as one could see, we were very keen that they should say. That village was in the area delegated to one of my battalions. But I, as the Brigade Commander, felt that it was such an important place and important for the peace process that we keep those 300 villagers there and in their village, that I personally went to the village on many occasions, personally led the negotiations with the people to try and persuade them to stay. So I engaged myself in that area because it was so important that we got that right, so far as I was concerned. Now, in doing that, I hadn't assumed command from the Battalion Commander in that area, but I was supporting him and putting myself into it to try and lend greater authority, try to persuade the people to stay. If you like, at that moment in my area, that village of Majdan was the main effort, and, therefore, I as the higher Commander was there, in the same way that it does not surprise me that General Mladic turned up in the area of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, let's move on to the next section of your evidence which concerns the movement of the population from Potocari to the Bosniak-controlled area in Kladanj and Tuzla. Now, from general principles, if you, as a military Commander, enter an area with a military force and a large group of civilians gather in a small location as a result of the entrance of that military force, what is your obligation to those civilians as a military Commander, as far as you understand?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT
utterances.text: Well, under the Geneva Convention, the military are obliged to assume certain responsibilities for civilians when those civilians can no longer look after themselves. When their own civilian municipal or local government structure can no longer look after them, then it falls to the military to carry out that function. The minimum requirements of that function would be to provide food, water, shelter, and medical support.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you state in your report that you, as a military Commander, would actually have a duty of care to those people. Is that an obligation that you see as applying in this situation in Potocari?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT
utterances.text: Very much so. The status of those civilians under the Geneva Convention becomes one of protected persons by definition that they can no longer protect themselves, they can no longer look after themselves, and therefore from a military point of view, like it or not, then you have this duty of care which, by the Geneva Convention, is vested upon you and you must do the things that I have just described: food, shelter, water, medical care, and freedom from harassment; the basic provision of human rights.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Usher, if you could place this exhibit, this large VRS Drina Corps structure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, what I'd like you to do now is to explain to Their Honours, from your own understanding as a military Commander, what is required to move 25.000 to 30.000 people a distance of about 50 miles? What kind of resources, what kind of planning? In your report, I know you've used NATO references for the Staff Branches involved but what I would like you to do is to address this VRS Drina Corps structure. Explain to the Judges the planning involved, the resources involved, and the Staff Branches which, in your opinion, would have been engaged in planning and executing this kind of operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So, Mr. Usher, if you could give the General the microphone. THE USHER: Of course.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There's a pointer, I think, there, General, you can use.

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Your Honour, I think to move 25.000 to 30.000 people, it must be realised, is a significant military -- undertaking by anybody, and if being conducted by the military, it requires quite a lot of planning. We've already, I think, said in the course of the examination so far that this was done relatively quickly, and therefore the more quickly a thing is done, the greater degree of planning that has to be involved. From this outline diagram of the Drina Corps structure, I would see quite a number of Staff Branches inevitably being involved. Because we're moving large numbers, 25.000 to 30.000, through a war zone, the Operations Staff would inevitably have to be involved to make sure that the routes that were going to be selected and the locations that were going to be used were free from where active combat was going on. So the Operations Staff would be very closely involved. The Intelligence Staff, naturally, would play a part with the Operations Staff to make sure that the picture was an accurate picture and that the people were not going to be placed in any greater degree of threat than they already were. On this side, the Department for Rear Services, a large number of the Staff Branches would be involved. The Quartermaster Service here should provide water and food for the people. The Transportation Service would undoubtedly be the one that would coordinate buses and trucks to move the people. We've got the Medical Service here that, for a proper operation, should be required to provide first-aid points as a minimum to provide care for people while they are in transit. Of course, already having drawn attention to three or four of the branches on this side and a couple of branches on this side, they all feed up in the hierarchy to the Chief of Staff of a formation like that who would have to oversee the operational aspects, and also in conjunction with the heads, in this case the Department for Rear Services, to ensure that there was integration on this side with the activities on this side and that the whole thing was a comprehensive and properly conducted military operation. I can't countenance how you could move 25.000 to 30.000 people other than it being properly planned, and particularly done so in a short period of time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please, General, if you would like to take your seat. Thank you. General, this is a question that you've essentially already answered but I'm going to ask you again: Is it possible that this operation could have taken place without the involvement or the knowledge of the Corps staff, the Chief of Staff, and the Commander? Is that possible?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT
utterances.text: No. I couldn't countenance it, of that magnitude, taking place. I mean, the way I rather envisage the situation of the Drina Corps area over these few days is it was a very busy place. One had an attack that had just been mounted on Srebrenica; we know of another attack being planned on Zepa; we have the 28th Muslim Division having broken out, heading off towards his own line, a large column, which is a major issue in its own right; then we have another bunch of 25.000 to 30.000 people who are going to be moved to behind their own lines to a place of safety. There were a tremendous amount of moving parts in the Drina Corps at that stage, and unless that had been coordinated -- obviously it had been coordinated and coordinated properly -- I think it would have been chaos fairly quickly. The only way that it could have been coordinated was as a result of the Corps staff and the Corps headquarters having visibility of everything that was going on and making sure that there was all deconfliction [sic] and that all the missions were accomplished successfully. It's a long answer to your short question. But, no, I can't envisage that number of people being moved without knowledge and visibility and, indeed, sort of proactive intervention by the Corps staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: In fact, if the witness could be shown Prosecutor's Exhibit 435, which I think is just a small demonstration of one of the elements that you've just addressed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is an intercepted conversation between General Krstic and Lieutenant Colonel Krsmanovic who was in, I think, the Department for Rear Services of the Drina Corps staff. What does this conversation represent to you?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT
utterances.text: Well, it's a detailed and very clear confirmation of the general point I've been trying to make. What we have here, and it happens to be General Krstic speaking in this paragraph here, giving quite clear orders that 50 buses in total from those various towns that are shown in the first two lines are to be at the stadium in Bratunac by 1700. They were needed there because a large number of people had to be moved. Whatever position General Krstic was in at the time, at that time, at that date, quite clearly he was involved in the process, as one would expect, because it needed Corps-level coordination to get the right number of vehicles, the right transport available, to achieve this large transportation problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If the witness could be shown Prosecutor's Exhibit 459, which essentially ends the movement of the civilian population.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is a report to the Command of the Drina Corps from Colonel Jankovic, a Main Staff officer who we mentioned earlier. What does this particular document say to you, General?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT
utterances.text: It's essentially a report to the Drina Corps Command reporting that this deportation operation had effectively been completed. In fact, the first line says: "The evacuation of the entire Muslim population from the former enclave of Srebrenica was completed." So it was a subordinate officer who had some responsibilities for part of this operation, informing his higher headquarters that the operation that had been ordered was now successfully completed. It, rather, bears out what I was saying: that it was a major operation that needed Corps-level control, and it had had it and now it was being reported back upwards.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, one last point that we asked you to address in your report was the matter of interrogation of men who were separated at Potocari. What evidence have you seen from the documents that you've looked at, from Mr. Butler's report, what evidence have you seen of organised interrogation? How do you understand, as a military Commander, how that kind of activity takes place?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT
utterances.text: Frankly, I haven't seen much evidence. Rather, as I was suggesting earlier in answer to one of Your Honour's questions, that it may well have been a reasonable thing, following your own logic, to separate the men from, obviously, the non-combatants and to interrogate them to try and identify those who might have been guilty, in someone's judgement, of previous misdemeanors. But if you're going to do that, then a full degree of organisation is required to be put in place. I would have thought that at least to establish the identity of an individual, it's going to take a number of minutes, and if it's going to be done over a relatively short period of time, you've got to have quite a large number of interrogation or questioning teams. A lot of organisation has got to go into that process. From material that's been made available to me and the video film that I've seen, there doesn't appear to have been a comprehensive attempt made to carry out a proper interrogation, which can be the only real legitimate process for separating the men from the women. Indeed, I have seen evidence to suggest that far from trying to establish the identity of individuals, identity papers were being taken off people. That seems to be rather counterintuitive to the notion of trying to see who was who and who might have been involved previously in misdemeanors earlier in the war. So I don't see evidence of a systematic process of interrogation.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, I don't know whether you feel this is an appropriate time to finish for today, since we're now moving into another area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Cayley, I think this would be an appropriate time for a break. I think that the Chamber is ready to make a ruling, but we will do it tomorrow so that we do not prolong today's work. So we will make our ruling at the beginning of our session tomorrow morning. Tomorrow morning at 9.30. The hearing stands adjourned.
